lesson.title: Predictable Errors: What Cognitive Biases Reveal About the Thinking Mind
lesson.summary: Cognitive biases are systematic, predictable patterns of error in thinking that arise from relying on heuristics and other mental shortcuts, showing that mistakes in judgment are often not random but follow consistent, well documented patterns rooted in how the mind normally processes information.
lesson.body:
A cognitive bias is a systematic, predictable pattern of deviation from accurate or rational judgment, one that shows up consistently across many people and many situations rather than occurring as a one-off, random mistake. This consistency is what makes cognitive biases so interesting and so useful to study: if judgment errors were purely random, they would be nearly impossible to anticipate or correct, but because cognitive biases follow recognizable patterns, psychologists can describe them, predict when they are likely to occur, and in some cases design ways to reduce their influence.

Cognitive biases are closely tied to heuristics, the mental shortcuts covered earlier, because most well documented biases arise directly from relying on a heuristic in a situation where it happens to produce a misleading answer. The representativeness heuristic reliably produces a bias toward ignoring base rates in favor of resemblance to a prototype. The availability heuristic reliably produces a bias toward overestimating the frequency of vivid or memorable events and underestimating the frequency of mundane ones. Mental set reliably produces a bias toward sticking with a familiar strategy even when a better one is available. In each case, the bias is not a separate malfunction but the predictable downstream consequence of a normally useful shortcut being applied in a situation where it stops being reliable.

Beyond the biases tied to specific heuristics already discussed, psychologists have documented many other consistent patterns, one of the most familiar being confirmation bias, the tendency to search for, notice, and remember information that supports what a person already believes, while overlooking or discounting information that contradicts it. Someone convinced that a particular brand of car is unreliable will tend to notice and remember every breakdown they hear about involving that brand, while barely registering the far more common instances of that same brand running trouble free for years, simply because the breakdown stories confirm an existing belief and the trouble free stories do not.

It is worth emphasizing that cognitive biases are not evidence of poor intelligence or careless thinking; they are the ordinary byproduct of a mind that is built to make fast, efficient judgments using limited time and limited information, the same underlying trade-off that shows up in perception through top-down processing and perceptual sets. A fully bias free judgment process, one that gathered and weighed every relevant piece of information with no shortcuts at all, would be far too slow to be useful for most everyday decisions. Cognitive biases are the cost of that speed, and understanding them does not eliminate them, since they operate automatically, but it does make it possible to build in deliberate checks, such as actively seeking out disconfirming evidence, in situations where accuracy matters more than speed.

Confirmation bias, base rate neglect, and the pull of mental set are just a few entries in a much longer catalog of documented cognitive biases, and two of the most widely recognized examples involve how people reason about chance and about past investment: the gambler's fallacy, a systematic error in judging random, independent events, and the sunk cost fallacy, a systematic error in letting past investment influence a decision that should really only depend on future outcomes.
